extracted.intended_audience: pre-IPO company executives, investor-relations/communications teams, and corporate counsel
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for companies on what they may and may not say during the SEC-imposed IPO quiet period, plus practical tips for listing-day interviews and media engagement surrounding an IPO.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of IPO quiet period
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC requires that from the time a company begins the IPO process they operate in a 'quiet period.' Beginning that process is generally defined as the point at which they retain investment bankers for that purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulators want all relevant information of interest to potential investors to be contained in one place — the Prospectus (S-1 filing) — which the SEC reviews and approves. The definition can be unclear in practice, but treat the quiet period as starting when bankers are retained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contain material information in the prospectus (S-1)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any new or material information about the company provided outside the S-1 (e.g., media interviews, press releases, social media, conference presentations) during the quiet period is considered a violation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that substantive business information, performance metrics, future prospects, or major developments are disclosed only in the prospectus while in the quiet period. Even confidential employee communications are subject to these guidelines (example: Groupon internal memo sanction).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted 'normal course of business' communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies are allowed to continue 'normal course of business' external marketing and typical internal communications during the quiet period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This generally covers basic press releases, product announcements, data reports, new-hire announcements, and routine marketing. However, whether a communication qualifies as 'normal course' depends on prior practice — if you didn't regularly do these things before filing, it's harder to claim they're normal course now.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substantive commentary on business performance and prospects
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary restrictions cover substantive commentary about the business, its performance or financial results, future prospects, or major developments (e.g., new customers, litigation updates, entering new markets).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: All such business information needs to be contained in the S-1 and not discussed publicly elsewhere. Executive and board comments are particularly scrutinized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledging the IPO process vs. commenting on the offering
rubrics_metrics.description: Publicly acknowledging that the company is in the IPO process is sometimes done, but commenting on the offering itself is generally frowned upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you acknowledge the filing, avoid commentary about the offering terms or progress. Keep any acknowledgment high-level and factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Educate executives, board, and employees on communication rules
rubrics_metrics.description: It is critical to educate the executive team, board, and employee base about the rules and restrictions on communication once pursuing an IPO is public knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear guidance and training so that spokespeople avoid making unapproved statements. Remind staff that even internal communications can trigger regulatory issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coach spokespeople and avoid executive interviews pre-IPO
rubrics_metrics.description: Spokespeople who may engage in media interviews or public events need careful coaching on answering questions and avoiding prohibited topics; for senior executives, the advice is to refrain from interviews prior to the company’s IPO.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because senior executives are heavily scrutinized and it's nearly impossible to avoid slip-ups, limiting their public appearances minimizes risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing day interviews: permitted but sensitive
rubrics_metrics.description: Following pricing and listing of the stock, the company remains in a quiet period for another few weeks, but listing day interviews with tier-one financial outlets and select publications have become customary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the listing day as a branding and business-development opportunity but prepare carefully to navigate sensitive regulatory boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare comprehensive Q&A for interviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully prepare for interviews with a comprehensive Q&A session that anticipates typical IPO interview questions (e.g., 'Tell me about the roadshow', 'How do you feel about the offering price').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop suggested answers (for example: 'If we execute our business plan, we are confident the stock price will take care of itself over time') and rehearse them with spokespeople.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop planned responses for questions that cross the line
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare planned responses for questions that would cross regulatory lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use safe fallback language such as, 'We’ve stated X in our filing, and we look forward to updating investors and the public in the future.' Have these scripts pre-approved and aligned with counsel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Align all messaging and responses with the prospectus
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure all key messaging and planned responses are aligned with statements in the prospectus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cross-check interviews and talking points against the S-1 to avoid inconsistencies that could be problematic with the SEC or investors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for questions about prospectus risk factors and mitigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipate media questions about 'risk factors' highlighted in the prospectus and prepare responses that explain how the company is mitigating those risks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame answers to communicate mitigation strategies and avoid providing new material facts not disclosed in the S-1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult counsel and underwriters on interview timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Consult with company counsel as well as the underwriters and underwriters’ counsel to determine whether to pursue listing day interviews prior to trading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision-making about interviews should involve legal and underwriting teams to balance marketing benefits against regulatory risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain consistent messaging regardless of stock movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Prepare to give the same interview whether the stock trades up 50% or down 50%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid reactive or materially different statements based on short-term trading that could create new disclosures or misleading impressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit number of interviews and spokespeople
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit the total number of interviews and spokespeople to ensure messaging stays tight and manageable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The roadshow is exhausting; fewer interviews and controlled spokespeople reduce the risk of inconsistent messaging or mistakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your interviewer and prep them in advance
rubrics_metrics.description: Know your interviewer and make sure they are informed about the company in advance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brief interviewers to reduce the chance they ask unpredictable questions that could lead to problematic disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stick to the script and avoid creating new news
rubrics_metrics.description: The interview should not 'create new news' — the IPO itself is the news; interviews should guide the narrative without introducing new material information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use interviews to inform the story and shine a light on the IPO event, not to announce unfiled material facts or changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of missteps: potential cooling-off period and reputational harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Missteps in communication can result in a 'cooling off period' mandated by the SEC, delaying IPO plans, and can cause investors to doubt the company's readiness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat communications as a regulatory and reputational risk; careful planning and experienced execution help maximize brand exposure without stepping out of line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish active communication practices before filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should establish a practice of active communication prior to entering the IPO process so routine announcements can credibly be treated as 'normal course' during the quiet period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don’t regularly send press releases or do media interviews before filing, it will be difficult to treat those activities as normal course during the quiet period.
